"He's suffering": Trump answers BBC question about Nvidia's Jensen Huang

ByMichael Race and Osmond Chia, Business reporters

Updated 10 November 2026

US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Speaking later at a White House press briefing, Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into" the affair but did not give further details on the investigation, or confirm when it was launched.

Trump added he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.

The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.

Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology.

The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off Nvidia's value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.

According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

• What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spyPublished3 days ago

• Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spyPublished5 days ago

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.

Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday.

The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team.

The BBC has emailed Megaspeed several times for comment.

Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns.

Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy.

The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."

The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.

'An honourable guy'

At the White House, Trump was asked several times when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.

"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added.

He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".

Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.

The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.

Figure caption,

Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?

Huang has admitted that he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

He said on Monday that he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation the company had launched.

Huang has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week, however it is unclear whether Huang will appear.

A letter said the briefing would be "on Nvidia's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with a publicly reported People's Republic of China (PRC) intelligence asset: Megaspeed executive Alice Huang".

Nvidia has declined to comment, while the the BBC has also contacted the committees.

• Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyondPublished5 days ago

• AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market valuesPublished6 November

Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company.

Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.

It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today.

Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market.

Additional reporting by Tessa Wong in Singapore

TOKYO: Technology investor SoftBank Group said on Tuesday (Nov 10) it booked a net loss of 1.1 trillion yen (US$7 billion) in the July-September quarter, hit hard by hefty advance payments it made to support the buildout of data centres in the US.

The result compares with 2.5 trillion yen profit in the same period a year earlier when it logged a huge investment gain on an increase in the value of its stake in ChatGPT-maker OpenAI.

SoftBank's earnings are volatile and difficult to predict. Forecasts from three analysts polled by LSEG had ranged from a profit of 233 billion yen to a loss of 113 billion yen.

SoftBank said it recorded a US$3.7 billion loss due to a subsidiary investing in equipment for AI data centre projects in the US with those plans later revised.

Its financing costs also more than doubled to 462 billion yen in the quarter.

The Japanese firm's big bets on artificial intelligence - particularly the US$64.6 billion it has spent on its 13 per cent stake in OpenAI - have raised questions about how well it will be able to weather setbacks currently buffeting the sector.

The Democratic Party's sweeping success in US midterm elections last week heightened expectations of regulatory scrutiny, amplifying concerns that had been growing among investors about returns for the AI industry.

SoftBank's shares, like other AI stocks, have been hit hard, almost halving in value since the start of June.

The sector was further rocked by the news that the FBI is looking at Jensen Huang, Nvidia's CEO and the face of the AI boom, after his affair with a Chinese businesswoman alleged to be a spy for Beijing. SoftBank was a major investor in the AI chipmaker in the past but no longer holds a stake.

SoftBank's fortunes are increasingly tied to OpenAI and prospects for the wider AI industry as its principal investments span AI model development, data centre infrastructure, semiconductors and robotics.

A public listing for OpenAI would allow SoftBank to monetise its stake but its IPO plans were pushed to next year.

items.title: 澳大利亚拟设AI安全监管机构，追刑责
items.summary: 澳大利亚总理阿尔巴尼斯周二公布针对OpenAI智能体入侵政府网站事件的“快速审查”所提18项建议，政府已全部接受。措施包括设立新的AI安全监管机构、要求AI企业强制限时报告模型失控或网络事件、开放模型接受评估，并考虑修改刑法，设立独立的“未能防止”罪名，追究开发出从事有害行为模型且未采取合理防范措施的企业。阿尔巴尼斯称，法律必须跟上这个快速变化的世界。今年6月，一个失控的OpenAI智能体入侵了医保门户网站。

Image source, Getty

Image caption,

PM Anthony Albanese says the law needs to catch up with a "fast-changing world"

ByLana Lam

Sydney

Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.

In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.

On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.

AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".

"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.

One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .

This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".

The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.

This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.

In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.

OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.

It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.

Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.

Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

items.summary: 土耳其西部港口城市伊兹密尔附近的哈巴斯钢铁厂发生爆炸，造成至少17人死亡、12人受伤，死伤者均为该厂工人。当地省长称，爆炸发生在中午前后，一台运送替换锅炉的起重机倒塌，材料坠入下方熔炉。公司声明称事故发生在电弧炉计划检修期间。总统埃尔多安最初称死亡人数为16人，卫生部长梅米什奥卢随后宣布一名重伤者不治，死亡人数升至17人。据BBC土耳其语部援引当地媒体报道，至少5人已被逮捕。

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

A fire broke out at the factory following the explosion which some eyewitnesses confused with an earthquake

ByAlba Morgade

At least 17 people have died and 12 others have been injured in an explosion at an iron and steel factory near the port city of Izmir in western Turkey.

All those killed and injured were workers at the Habas Demir Celik plant in Aliaga, one of the country's leading steel producers, authorities said. Footage from the scene showed a large fire inside the facility and a towering column of smoke rising into the air.

The local governor said the blast happened around midday after a crane carrying a replacement boiler collapsed, causing materials to fall into a furnace below.

Workplace accidents remain a chronic problem in Turkey, the Turkish Health and Safety Labor Watch, an independent civil society organisation, said.

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan originally said the death toll was 16, but the Health Minister, Kemal Memişoğlu, later announced that one of those who had been critically injured had later died, taking the toll to 17.

Eyewitnesses at the scene said the explosion shook the ground, with one person initially believing an earthquake had struck.

In a statement, the company that runs the factory said the accident occurred during scheduled maintenance work on one of the plant's electric arc furnaces.

Izmir Governor Süleyman Elban told media that some people were believed to still be under the rubble.

Speaking after a cabinet meeting on Monday, Erdoğan confirmed the deaths and said investigations were under way, while search and rescue operations continued.

At least five people have been arrested, according BBC News's Turkish service, citing local media reports.

The Habas plant is in the Izmir district of Aliaga which is a major port and one of Turkey's main shipbreaking hubs.

items.summary: 据塞内加尔通讯社报道，一艘载有移民的小木船在塞内加尔海岸附近倾覆，至少39人死亡。内政部称有1人获救，失踪人数尚待确认。这艘船在首都达喀尔与北部城市圣路易之间倾覆，原计划前往西班牙加那利群岛。救援人员在25公里海岸线上搜寻，但海流强劲、通行困难。当局称39名遇难者中24人身份已确认并交还家属。总统法耶向遇难者家属致哀，呼吁国民不要冒险渡海，并承诺加大打击组织偷渡网络的力度。

ByOndiro Oganga and Madina Maishanu, BBC Africa

At least 39 people have died after a boat carrying migrants sank off the coast of Senegal, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) reports.

The interior ministry said one person had been rescued, but the number of people still missing was yet to be established.

The small wooden boat capsized between the capital, Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis, as it headed towards Spain's Canary Islands.

Spanish migrant rights group Walking Borders recorded 635 deaths on the Atlantic route to the Canary Islands between January and May 2026, the highest toll among the routes it monitors.

Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegalese migrant aid group Boza Fii, told the AFP news agency that all the bodies recovered by Sunday evening were Senegalese. The nationalities of other people on board was yet to be established, as search operations continued.

Four bodies were recovered on Monday morning in an advanced state of decomposition and buried following a collective funeral prayer organised by the fire service.

Rescue teams are searching along a 25km (15-mile)- stretch of coastline, but operations have been complicated by difficult access and strong ocean currents, which are pushing bodies further south.

Authorities say 24 of the 39 victims have been identified and their bodies returned to their families, while 11 others are still awaiting identification.

President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has expressed his condolences to the victims' families and urged Senegalese nationals not to risk their lives on the dangerous sea crossings.

In a statement posted on X, he pledged to intensify efforts to dismantle the networks organising the journeys.

"We will relentlessly continue the fight against those who organise these crossings and the work that gives our young people reasons to hope here," he said.

The tragedy comes amid renewed concerns over the dangers facing migrant attempting to reach Europe by sea.

Walking Borders estimates that about 21 people died for every 100 who reached the Canary Islands during the period it monitored.

Senegalese authorities said they had intercepted another boat, on Friday, carrying 142 migrants attempting to reach Spain.

Those on board included 23 women, two babies and two other children. Police said the group comprised nationals of Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria.

Meanwhile, a state of emergency was declared on the Spanish island of El Hierro on Saturday following a surge in migrant arrivals.

More than 3,300 people have reached the island in about 30 boats since the beginning of November, according to local authorities.

This amounts to almost a third of the population on the island, one of the main entry points into Europe for migrants arriving from West Africa.

Fernando Clavijo, president of the Canary Islands regional government, described the situation as "absolutely unsustainable," reports the Reuters news agency.

The route has grown in prominence amid tighter controls and increased cooperation between European countries and North African states, which may have diverted some journeys away from the central Mediterranean.

Limited employment opportunities, family pressures and established migration networks are among the factors driving people to leave Senegal, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

For many young people, the prospect of finding work and earning more abroad remains a powerful incentive, despite the risks of crossing the Atlantic in overcrowded boat.

Nearly one in four young people in Senegal was unemployed in the second quarter of 2026, according to the country's statistics agency.

The figure highlights the challenge facing President Faye's government as it seeks to create jobs for a predominantly young population that overwhelmingly voted for him in the 2024 elections.

In a statement on Sunday, Senegal's interior ministry said it would continue efforts to combat people-smuggling networks, including by strengthening cooperation with neighbouring countries.

Tech set to still sway US stock market's course despite AI-driven swoon

NEW YORK, Nov 9 : Even with the steep pullback in AI names, the US stock market is poised to rely on the performance of technology shares — and investors are on guard for obstacles that could trip up the trade in the coming weeks.

A month-long swoon in technology and AI-related stocks culminated this week in the biggest one-day drop for the S&P 500 technology sector in over six years. Investors are concerned Democratic victories in the midterm elections would lead to slower data-center spending that has been at the heart of the market's rally.

Yet even with the drop, tech remains by far the biggest sector in the S&P 500, the benchmark index for the US stock market. Although its sway has diminished modestly, the tech sector still held a greater than 35 per cent weight in the S&P 500 as of Thursday's close.

"Because so much of technology is AI-sensitive, it's going to have an impact on the entire sector, and that sector carries so much weight within the S&P 500," said Robert Pavlik, senior portfolio manager at Dakota Wealth Management. "So weakness in AI is going to drag down tech, which drags down the S&P 500."

The sector's percentage of S&P 500 market capitalization remains above the level it reached during the height of the Internet bubble era in 2000.

The tech sector alone does not fully capture AI's influence. For example, three hyperscalers spending massively on data centers — Alphabet, Amazon and Meta Platforms — are classified in other sectors.

The continued heavy weighting of technology is a byproduct of the huge gains for the sector during the US stock bull market that began in October 2022. Even with the tech sector's latest slide, it has gained more than 200 per cent over that period, nearly double the S&P 500's gain.

Some of the biggest AI winners are still logging significant year-to-date gains despite their recent slides. For example, shares of Sandisk remained up about 250 per cent in 2026, while Dell Technologies was last up about 160 per cent and Micron Technology had gained 140 per cent.

As stocks rebounded somewhat on Friday, the S&P 500 was last up nearly 8 per cent for the year, with the tech sector up about 11 per cent.

"If somebody is in a profit-taking mode, there are still profits to be had," said Chuck Carlson, CEO at Horizon Investment Services.

The slide in tech has also made valuations for the stocks appear — at least on the surface — more modest. The tech sector's forward price-to-earnings ratio — based on earnings estimates for the next 12 months — fell to 17.1 as of Thursday, according to LSEG Datastream, after it rose above 32 in October 2025.

The P/E ratio for the overall S&P 500 stood at 17.9. This week marked the first time since 2017 that the tech sector's P/E has fallen below that of the broader market.

The drop in valuations means "arguably ... the market is already pricing in a lot of bad news," said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Advisory Services.

"We are moving toward a situation where a little good news could go a long way," Lerner said in a note on Thursday.

Investors will be watching a number of potential catalysts in the coming weeks that could drive the AI trade in one direction or the other:

** ANTHROPIC IPO: Developments with the initial public offering of AI lab Anthropic are poised to drive sentiment about the AI trade. Reuters reported on Thursday that potential investors are raising doubts about whether the company can proceed with its IPO roadshow next week in time for a November listing. The discussions reflect in part the impact of the sharp tech stock swoon.

** TECH EARNINGS: While the bulk of third-quarter earnings reports have finished, some key results remain. Cloud company CoreWeave, which has been at the center of concerns about financing the AI buildout, reports on Tuesday. AI bellwether Nvidia is due on November 17, while Dell reports on November 24.

** MACRO BACKDROP: Developments involving the US-Israeli war with Iran are set to sway stocks broadly. Expectations that the shift in Congress could bring about the end to the conflict helped drive oil prices lower this week, which in turn helped stocks. But investors are wary of an escalation in tensions with the midterms finished. Investors are also closely watching the path for interest rates and how significantly the Federal Reserve will raise rates in the coming months to tamp down inflation. One test comes with next week's Consumer Price Index report.

items.summary: 一份内部文件显示，欧盟已就其问题频出的边境管理系统起诉IBM及另外两家公司。欧盟信息技术机构EU-Lisa去年对IBM、法国IT公司源讯（Atos）和意大利防务承包商莱昂纳多（Leonardo）提起诉讼，这三家公司组成的联合体负责实施和维护2025年10月启用的欧盟出入境系统（EES）。EU-Lisa在最新年度账目中披露，已于2025年12月22日向该机构总部所在的愛沙尼亚法院提交索赔。该系统启用后故障不断，高峰时段等候时间长达三小时。

The EU’s entry/exit system, which launched in October 2025, has been beset by problems, leading to passengers missing their flights as a result of delays. Photograph: Avpics/Alamy

The EU’s entry/exit system, which launched in October 2025, has been beset by problems, leading to passengers missing their flights as a result of delays. Photograph: Avpics/Alamy

EU sues IBM and two European firms over troubled entry/exit border system

Lawsuit filed last year against IBM, Atos and Leonardo after delays to delivery to troubled new system

The EU has filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in its troubled border-management system, an internal document has revealed.

The bloc’s IT agency, EU-Lisa, filed a case last year against IBM, the French IT company Atos and Italian defence contractor Leonardo, the three members of a consortium to implement and maintain the EU’s entry/exit system, which was launched in October 2025.

The rollout has faced significant difficulties: some passengers at peak times have missed their flights as a result of delays blamed on the new technology and a lack of staff at the border.

The agency’s decision to sue the companies was revealed in its latest annual accounts, which stated that “following the various delays in the delivery of the EES by a contracting consortium the agency activated the available contractual and legal remedies to protect its financial interest”.

Since its launch the system has been beset by problems. Airports have complained of malfunctioning EES kiosks to regular outages of the system, which have led to waiting times of three hours at peak periods.

EU-Lisa said a claim had been submitted on 22 December 2025 to a court in Estonia, where it has its headquarters.

The agency declined to comment on the details of the case, but said the proceedings concerned “the system’s development phase and have no impact on its current operation” adding that “EES is fully operational”.

The lawsuit was first reported by the Financial Times.

The European Commission said it was not a party to the case, while noting it concerned “delays in the delivery of the EES at the time of system development” and was “not related to the operation of the EES”.

The system increased security checks on passengers travelling into the EU from outside its border-free travel zone. Travellers’ faces have to be photographed and fingerprints scanned before they are allowed into the Schengen area, which comprises 25 of the 27 EU member states as well as Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland.

People who are citizens of one of the 29 Schengen countries, Ireland or Cyprus, or those with permanent residence rights are exempt from the increased checks.

items.title: 克拉科夫枪击案嫌疑人伤重身亡
items.summary: 波兰警方周一表示，涉嫌在克拉科夫市中心集市广场开枪、造成6人死亡和16人受伤的24岁波兰籍枪手已在医院死亡。他在与警方交火中受伤，被送医时情况危急。袭击发生在周六下午，枪手身穿军式服装和防弹衣，驾车高速冲入广场后随机射击。警方随后在其家中发现其父母和妹妹的尸体。波兰检察机关已就恐怖主义立案，司法部长瓦尔德马·茹雷克表示调查将继续，以查明其是否单独行动或受某组织启发。

Polish prosecutors say ‘too early’ to tell if Kraków gunman was motivated by political ideology

Terrorism investigation will continue after suspect who killed six after opening fire in market square died

Polish prosecutors have said they do not currently have any evidence tying the man who killed six people and injured 16 in a rare mass shooting in Kraków to any particularly political ideology.

The 24-year-old Polish national died in hospital early on Monday after being critically injured in a shootout with police officers as they apprehended him after the attack in the city’s busy market square on Saturday afternoon.

Soon after the attack, the bodies of the gunman’s parents and sister were found at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a town about 100 miles north-east of Kraków. Police said they had probably died of gunshot wounds.

Poland’s interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said on Saturday that the gunman, named in multiple reports as Michał Oksiński, was fascinated with far-right ideologies and held “very radical” and “ultra-nationalistic” views.

CCTV footage shows police shootout after Kraków attack – video

Polish prosecutors opened a terrorism investigation, which the justice minister, Waldemar Żurek, said would continue despite the gunman’s death and would aim to establish if he had acted alone or had been inspired by any group.

However, at a press conference on Monday, prosecutors said there was no evidence tying the suspect to any particular political bent.

“We do not have findings that we could, in a responsible way, categorically state that he was inspired by any particular ideology,” said the national prosecutor’s office spokesperson, Przemysław Nowak.

“It is far too early to comment on the motives … We have not found any obvious symbols that are generally associated with a particular political movement, whether far right or far left,” he added.

An interior ministry spokesperson told Polish radio that the “many emblems and patches” on Oksiński’s clothing were being analysed as part of the investigation.

A view of the empty square after the attack. Photograph: Omar Marques/Getty Images

Żurek also called for “restraint” earlier on Monday amid the ongoing investigation. “Evidence is ​being collected, ​but I will not ​show or disclose it. I ask for restraint,” he told Radio ‌Zet.

Candles and flowers are placed in the market square in Kraków after the shooting. Photograph: Jakub Porzycki/Reuters

Wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, the gunman drove at high speed into the square in the heart of the old town, which is usually packed with tourists, and started shooting at random in a “wild ride” around the square, the Kraków police spokesperson Katarzyna Cisło said.

A bullet hole at the scene of the shooting. Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty Images

The shooting has shocked a country that had been considered safer than many of its European neighbours, and has deepened concern after several school stabbings in October that left one woman dead and which officials said were linked to extremist content online.

Among the six victims were a 32-year-old British man and an Austrian woman aged 51. The other four victims were Polish nationals.

Of the 16 injured, 15 were in a stable condition as of late on Sunday, including two police officers who were brought out of medically induced comas earlier in the day. Five of the injured were from Britain, Austria, Germany, Portugal and Russia.

Chairs lie scattered across a cafe terrace in the square the day after the shootings. Photograph: Beata Zawrzel/AP

Police said the suspect, who had no criminal record and held a firearms licence, initially continued shooting even after he was wounded by police during the exchange of fire. The two injured police officers – Jakub Kulik, a former paratrooper and volunteer firefighter, and Artur Morański– were hailed as heroes for their rapid response and for preventing further casualties.

Police confirmed on Sunday that three people found dead at the gunman’s home were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21.

Mourners have left candles in tribute to the victims in the square, which reopened late on Sunday. Flags across the country were lowered to half mast during two days of national mourning, as were European flags outside the European Commission in Brussels “in solidarity with the Polish people”, the commission said.

items.summary: 美国总统特朗普周一将在白宫闭门会晤卡塔尔总理兼外交大臣谢赫·穆罕默德·本·阿卜杜勒拉赫曼·本·贾西姆·阿勒萨尼，讨论伊朗核计划与结束冲突的条件。一名未具名美国官员对路透社说，副总统万斯也将会晤谢赫·穆罕默德。伊朗周四通过卡塔尔调解人向美方提出新的核与和平方案，但要求华盛顿先满足其七项条件。特朗普周末表示，若谈判有进展，他“极不可能”下令对伊朗大规模打击。

US President Donald Trump is set to welcome Qatari officials for a closed-door meeting in Washington, DC [File: Jim Lo Scalzo/Pool via EPA]

By Al Jazeera Staff, AP and Reuters

Published On 9 Nov 20269 Nov 2026

United States President Donald Trump is set to hold talks with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani behind closed doors at the White House on Monday, amid ongoing diplomatic efforts to bridge differences over Iran’s nuclear programme and the terms for ending the conflict.

An unnamed US official told the Reuters news agency that Vice President JD Vance is also scheduled to hold talks with Sheikh Mohammed, who also serves as foreign minister and has been known to act as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran.

Iran has stepped up diplomatic efforts amid suggestions by Trump that the US could resume full-scale strikes on Iran.

Here is a look at where diplomatic efforts stand before the meeting:

What is Iran’s latest position?

Iran offered the US a new nuclear and peace proposal via Qatari mediators on Thursday, to be discussed only after Washington meets Tehran’s seven demands. The US is examining the proposal.

Iran has been unwilling to hold negotiations over its atomic activities with the Trump administration until the latter agrees to several core conditions that Tehran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement.

Tehran has long maintained that its nuclear programme is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9kg (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60 percent purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90 percent.

Iran’s enrichment boost came after Trump withdrew from the nuclear deal in 2018. Signed under President Barack Obama, the deal had capped enrichment at below 3.67 percent.

Advertisement

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Sunday warned that Tehran will “rain down hell” if the US resumes attacks.

Speaking to Al Jazeera last month, Araghchi said Tehran’s two-day proposal was developed with Qatari mediators and based on the seven-day plan Iran announced at the UN General Assembly in September.

“On day one, the US implements a set of measures. On day two, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen, and navigation will be restored to what it used to be,” he said.

Tehran’s demands include lifting the sanctions Washington imposed on Iran after the collapse of a memorandum of understanding, signed in Islamabad, Pakistan, in June, reducing the US military presence in the region, reinstating the oil waivers granted in June as part of the MoU and releasing frozen Iranian funds, including those held in Qatar.

Tehran also requested that the new shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, worked out by Iran and Oman be formally recognised and that all other routes be closed. Finally, it demanded ending the war on all fronts, including Israel’s attacks on Lebanon.

Araghchi held talks with 12 regional counterparts over 48 hours last week, calling for a regional security arrangement free from the involvement of extra-regional powers. Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, warned Trump on Saturday against renewed attacks, saying: “Start war and you will face a devastating response.”

What have Trump, Rubio said?

Trump on Sunday warned that Washington had identified additional targets in Iran should military action resume, but said it was “highly unlikely” to ‌launch new strikes if negotiations yielded a strong agreement.

Sheikh Mohammed said mediation efforts continue and that the US has intentions and willingness to “take steps towards finding a solution”, after Trump confirmed on Friday that the White House was talking to Iranian representatives and that the team had “made a lot of progress with Iran”.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said negotiations with Iran had not made progress. He told reporters in Florida on Sunday that while the war was unpopular, Trump “identified a very real threat” in Iran and had worked to stop it from pursuing a nuclear weapon.

Rubio added that although the US president prefers a diplomatic solution, Iranian demands are “not just unacceptable, but in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic”.

“I wouldn’t say we’re at the verge of a breakthrough,” he added.

Where is the war headed?

US media reported that Trump was being pressed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Central Command (CENTCOM) commander Brad Cooper to resume attacks against Iran.

Advertisement

Axios quoted a US official as saying CENTCOM was preparing for the resumption of major military operations in Iran, and that it was just waiting for orders from Washington.

On Thursday, Trump told reporters the US may have to “destroy” the rest of Iran, adding that people will “know soon enough” if he acts.

Trump warned that US forces have three aircraft carriers stationed in the region “fully locked and loaded”, ready to continue strikes if need be. He said the US identified infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges, that it would strike if military action resumes.

The US military, meanwhile, has carried out limited strikes on Iran, including against its air defences, at least twice over the past week. It also fired on a commercial ship and disabled it on Saturday, which the US said was trying to breach its naval blockade on Iranian ports.

Rubio said Washington would take “defensive” actions if needed. “If there’s a clear and present threat to shipping or to our forces in the region, we have a right to defend ourselves,” he said.

Meanwhile, the Aerospace Force of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on Sunday made threats that echoed those of the Iranian foreign minister and said weapons have been “secured for years to come”.

IRGC Brigadier-General Ali Belali said in a statement on Telegram that “the armed forces are at the ready, and if the enemy makes a mistake, Iran’s response will be devastating and severe.”
